# Missingness {#sec-missingness}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("_common.R")
```

R builds missing values into most of its vector types. Logical, integer, double, complex, and character vectors can all hold `NA`, and "in general any operation on an `NA` becomes an `NA`" [@r-intro, sec. 2.5]. Rust has no `NA`. An `i32` always holds an integer, and an `f64` always holds a floating-point value, though that value can be `NaN`. A value that might be absent has a different type, `Option`, and the compiler won't let you use it as if the value were there. This chapter compares `NA` with `Option`, shows how to get a value out of an `Option`, and maps R's `NULL` onto `Option` for optional arguments. The matching sections of the Rust book are "Defining an Enum", which introduces `Option`, and "Concise Control Flow with `if let` and `let...else`" [@rustbook, secs. 6.1, 6.3].

## `NA` in R

R has a separate `NA` for each vector type that can hold one. Plain `NA` is logical, and the other four have their own names:

```{r}
#| label: r-na-types
typeof(NA)
typeof(NA_integer_)
typeof(NA_real_)
typeof(NA_complex_)
typeof(NA_character_)
```

Each one is a value of its own type that R sets aside as a marker. @sec-types showed that `NA_integer_` is the smallest 32-bit integer. R's `NA_real_` is a special kind of `NaN` [@r-exts, sec. 5.10.3].

Because `NA` is a value of the vector's own type, arithmetic accepts it and passes it along:

```{r}
#| label: r-na-propagates
NA + 1
NA > 1
mean(c(1, NA, 3))
```

Nothing stops the calculation; the `NA` flows through to the result.

## `Option` in Rust

Rust writes a value that might be missing as an `Option`. An `Option<f64>` is either `Some` with an `f64` inside, or `None`:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-option
let reading: Option<f64> = Some(21.5);
let missing: Option<f64> = None;
println!("{:?}", reading);
println!("{:?}", missing);
```

The annotation on `missing` is required. The value `None` on its own doesn't say what kind of value is missing, and the compiler needs to know.

You've already seen `Option` twice. In @sec-vectors, `v.get(3)` returned `None` for a position past the end of a vector, and in @sec-types, `checked_add()` returned `None` when a sum overflowed. Both functions use `Option` to say "there may be no answer", and both make that visible in the type they return.

## An `Option` is not a number

An `Option<f64>` is not an `f64`, so you can't pass one where an `f64` is expected:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-option-mismatch
#| error: true
fn to_fahrenheit(celsius: f64) -> f64 {
    celsius * 1.8 + 32.0
}

fn main() {
    let reading: Option<f64> = Some(21.5);
    println!("{}", to_fahrenheit(reading));
}
```

Arithmetic fails the same way: `reading + 1.0` doesn't compile either. This is the central difference from R. In R, `NA` flows silently through a calculation. In Rust, a missing value stops at the first place that needs a real number, and you decide there what should happen.

## Getting the value out

In R, you check with `is.na()` before using a value. Rust's most direct tool is `if let`, which runs a block only when there's a value and gives that value a name:

```{r}
#| label: r-if-na
reading <- 21.5
if (!is.na(reading)) {
  cat("reading:", reading, "\n")
} else {
  cat("no reading\n")
}
```

```{rust}
#| label: rust-if-let
let reading: Option<f64> = Some(21.5);
if let Some(value) = reading {
    println!("reading: {value}");
} else {
    println!("no reading");
}
```

The pattern `if let Some(value) = reading` reads as "if `reading` is a `Some`, call the value inside it `value`". Inside the first block, `value` is a plain `f64`. Outside it, there's no `value` to misuse.

When a missing value should be replaced with a default, `unwrap_or()` is shorter. Rust's `is_none()` and `is_some()` answer the yes-or-no question that `is.na()` answers in R:

```{r}
#| label: r-replace-na
reading <- NA_real_
is.na(reading)
ifelse(is.na(reading), 0, reading)
```

```{rust}
#| label: rust-unwrap-or
let reading: Option<f64> = None;
println!("{}", reading.is_none());
println!("{}", reading.unwrap_or(0.0));
```

Rust computes the default before calling `unwrap_or()`, even when the value is there. That's harmless for `0.0`; for a default that's expensive to compute, @sec-closures introduces `unwrap_or_else()`, which computes it only when needed.

Finally, `expect()` takes the value out and stops the program with a panic if there isn't one. Use it when a missing value would mean a bug, the way you might use `stopifnot(!is.na(x))` in R:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-expect
#| error: true
let reading: Option<f64> = None;
println!("{}", reading.expect("sensor returned no reading"));
```

The message passed to `expect()` is what appears in the panic. A method called `unwrap()` does the same thing with a generic message. The compiler's suggestion in the earlier error was to call `expect()`, but that's only the right fix when `None` can't happen. @sec-enums covers `match`, the general tool for handling every case of an `Option`.

## Missing values in a vector

An R vector with missing values becomes a vector of `Option`s in Rust. R's summary functions take an `na.rm` argument:

```{r}
#| label: r-na-rm
readings <- c(1, NA, 3)
sum(readings, na.rm = TRUE)
sum(is.na(readings))
```

In Rust, the loop says what to do with each `None`:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-na-rm
let readings = vec![Some(1.0), None, Some(3.0)];
let mut total = 0.0;
let mut missing = 0;
for reading in readings {
    if let Some(value) = reading {
        total += value;
    } else {
        missing += 1;
    }
}
println!("total {total}, missing {missing}");
```

The type of `readings` is `Vec<Option<f64>>`, a vector in which every element might be missing. @sec-collections shows a shorter way to keep only the present values, with `filter_map()`.

::: {.callout-note title="An R habit to drop in Rust"}
In R, a numeric vector you receive might contain `NA`, so careful code checks with `is.na()` or passes `na.rm = TRUE` everywhere. In Rust, the type tells you. A `Vec<f64>` can't contain a missing value, so code that receives one doesn't need to check for missing values; `NaN` is a separate matter, which the next section takes up. Only a `Vec<Option<f64>>` can, and then the compiler makes you handle the `None`s. The checking moves from every function to the one place where missing values can occur.
:::

## `NaN` is not missing

R distinguishes a missing value, `NA`, from the result of an undefined calculation, `NaN`. R's `is.na()` is true for both, and `is.nan()` only for `NaN` [@r-intro, sec. 2.5]:

```{r}
#| label: r-nan
is.na(c(NA, NaN))
is.nan(c(NA, NaN))
```

Rust's `f64` has `NaN` but no `NA`, as @sec-types noted. Wrapping the value in an `Option` restores the distinction: `None` means the value was never recorded, and `Some(f64::NAN)` means it was computed and came out undefined:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-nan
let never_recorded: Option<f64> = None;
let undefined: Option<f64> = Some(f64::NAN);
println!("{:?}", never_recorded);
println!("{:?}", undefined);
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Where the analogy breaks"}
R's `na.rm = TRUE` removes `NaN` as well as `NA`, because `is.na()` is true for both. The loop in the previous section skips only `None`, so a `Some(f64::NAN)` would make its total `NaN`. To match R, skip the values for which `is_nan()` is true as well.
:::

## Missing logical values

R's logical type has three values: `TRUE`, `FALSE`, and `NA`. Logical operators handle `NA` where they can, but `if` can't:

```{r}
#| label: r-logical-na
#| error: true
NA || TRUE
NA && FALSE
if (NA) "yes"
```

A Rust `bool` has only `true` and `false`. A flag that might be missing is an `Option<bool>`, and `if` won't accept one, so you decide what `None` means first, for example with `flag.unwrap_or(false)`.

::: {.callout-warning title="Where the analogy breaks"}
R's `NA || TRUE` is `TRUE` because the answer doesn't depend on the missing value. Rust has no rule like that for `Option<bool>`: logical operators only work on `bool`. Any three-valued logic you want, you write yourself.
:::

## `NULL` and optional arguments

R's `NULL` is a different idea from `NA`. `NA` is a missing element inside a vector; `NULL` is the absence of an object altogether. Its most common use is as the default for an optional argument:

```{r}
#| label: r-null-argument
weighted <- function(x, weight = NULL) {
  if (is.null(weight)) {
    weight <- 1
  }
  x * weight
}
weighted(10)
weighted(10, weight = 2)
```

In Rust, an optional argument is an `Option`:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-option-argument
fn weighted(x: f64, weight: Option<f64>) -> f64 {
    let w = weight.unwrap_or(1.0);
    x * w
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", weighted(10.0, None));
    println!("{}", weighted(10.0, Some(2.0)));
}
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Where the analogy breaks"}
Rust has no default arguments and no named arguments. The caller always passes every argument, in order, so leaving out the weight means writing `None` explicitly.
:::

R's `NULL` also shows up when you ask a list for an element it doesn't have: `x[["b"]]` on a list without a `b` returns `NULL`. Use `[[` rather than `$` for this: `$` matches partial names, so `x$b` returns an element named `beta`. Rust's hash maps answer the same question with `None` (@sec-collections).

::: {.callout-note title="R refresher: NA, NaN, and NULL" collapse="true"}
The three behave differently in ways that matter when you translate code:

```{r}
#| label: r-refresher-null
length(NA)
length(NULL)
c(1, NA, 3)
c(1, NULL, 3)
```

`NA` is a value of length one that holds a place in a vector. `NULL` has length zero and disappears when combined with other values. `NaN` is an ordinary double that comes from calculations such as `0/0` [@r-intro, sec. 2.5]. In Rust terms, `NA` is closest to `None` inside a vector of `Option`s, `NULL` is closest to `None` as a whole argument or result, and `NaN` is `f64::NAN`.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Package developer notes: NA in compiled code" collapse="true"}
In C, missing integers, logicals, and strings are detected by comparing with `NA_INTEGER`, `NA_LOGICAL`, and `NA_STRING`. For doubles, `ISNA()` detects `NA`, while `ISNAN()` is true for both `NA` and `NaN` [@r-exts, sec. 5.10.3]. R's `NA_real_` is a `NaN` with a particular bit pattern, so a Rust function that receives R doubles as `f64` values sees `NA` as just another `NaN`: `is_nan()` is true for both. Telling them apart takes the same check `ISNA()` makes. @sec-extending-r shows how Rust code receives R vectors and their missing values.
:::

## Summary

| R | Rust |
|---------------------------|---------------------------|
| Most vector types have an `NA` | Plain types can't be missing; `Option<T>` can |
| `NA` flows through arithmetic | An `Option` can't be used as a number |
| `if (!is.na(x))` | `if let Some(value) = x` |
| `ifelse(is.na(x), 0, x)` | `x.unwrap_or(0.0)` |
| `is.na(x)` | `x.is_none()` |
| `stopifnot(!is.na(x))` | `x.expect("message")` |
| `sum(x, na.rm = TRUE)` | A loop that skips `None`, and `NaN` to match R |
| `NA` and `NaN` are both `is.na()` | `None` and `Some(f64::NAN)` are different values |
| `NA || TRUE` is `TRUE` | Logical operators need `bool`; decide what `None` means |
| `weight = NULL` as a default | `weight: Option<f64>`, passed as `None` |
